---
title: "Figure 1.2.2: Remittances to CA4 Countries"
---

![Python: `python/fig-1-2-2.py`](../images/python/fig-1-2-2.png)

Monthly growth of total remittances to four Central American countries (El
Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras and Nicaragua), year over year. The line is
the total for the four; the shaded area is the range between the country
with the lowest and the country with the highest growth in each month. A
wide band means the four countries are having very different experiences.

**New in this chart:** a min–max band. Otherwise it is a short and
straightforward script, a good example of a band chart. Compare
[Figure 15.2](fig-15-2.qmd), the same kind of chart with annual data.

## The data

Sheet `data`, 33 rows (monthly):

| category | Min | Min-Max Band | Total remittances |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2023-10-01 | 1.74 | 26.70 | 6.85 |

`Min-Max Band` is not the maximum. It is the *width* of the band, stacked on
top of `Min` in Excel. In the first row, the lowest growth rate is 1.74
percent and the highest is 1.74 + 26.70 = 28.44 percent.

The `category` column contains dates, one per month, always on the first of
the month.

## The script

### Dates and the band

```python
data = read_chart_data(STEM)
dates = pd.to_datetime(data["category"])

# In Excel the band is a stacked area: "Min" plus the "Min-Max Band" on top.
band_lower = data["Min"]
band_upper = data["Min"] + data["Min-Max Band"]
```

`pd.to_datetime()` makes sure the categories are real dates and not text,
whatever form they have in the Excel file. With dates on the x-axis,
matplotlib spaces the months by their actual length and can format the tick
labels as month names. See [Dates on the x-axis](../techniques.qmd#sec-dates).

The upper edge of the band is the minimum plus the width. Giving the two
edges their own names, `band_lower` and `band_upper`, makes the drawing code
below easier to read. See [Shaded bands](../techniques.qmd#sec-bands).

### The frame

`new_chart()` gets `caption_size=7.8`, smaller than usual, because the first
source line is long and must fit within the chart width. `bottom_gap=0.55`
leaves room for the month labels, which are written vertically.

### Drawing in layers

```python
ax.fill_between(dates, band_lower, band_upper, color="#FCE5D6", linewidth=0)
ax.axhline(0, color="#BFBFBF", linewidth=0.7)
ax.plot(dates, data["Total remittances"], color="#C55A11", linewidth=2.4,
        solid_capstyle="round", solid_joinstyle="round")
```

Order matters: each element is drawn over the previous ones.

1. **The band.** `ax.fill_between(x, lower, upper)` fills the area between
   the two edges, in a pale orange (`#FCE5D6`). `linewidth=0` removes the
   outline.
2. **A light grey line at zero.** The y-axis goes below zero, so a
   reference line shows where growth turns negative. It is drawn on top of
   the band, so it stays visible where the band covers zero, but in light
   grey (`#BFBFBF`), so it does not compete with the data.
3. **The remittances line**, in a dark orange of the same hue as the band.
   It is thicker than usual (2.4 points instead of about 1.8), because it is
   the only line in the chart. The round cap and join styles avoid sharp
   corners at the monthly turns. See [Line
   styles](../techniques.qmd#sec-line-styles).

### The x-axis: months

```python
ax.set_xlim(pd.Timestamp("2023-12-15"), pd.Timestamp("2026-06-15"))
ax.set_xticks(pd.date_range("2024-01-01", "2026-05-01", freq="2MS"))
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%b-%y"))
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelrotation=90, direction="in", length=2.8, pad=5)
```

- **Visible period.** The data start in October 2023, but the chart shows
  January 2024 to June 2026. Setting the x-limits is enough to hide the
  earlier months; there is no need to drop rows. With dates on the axis, the
  limits are dates too, written as `pd.Timestamp(...)`. The limits fall on
  the 15th, half a month before the first and after the last point shown.
- **Ticks.** `pd.date_range(start, end, freq="2MS")` makes a list of dates
  from January 2024 to May 2026. `"MS"` means *month start*, and `"2MS"`
  every second month start: Jan-24, Mar-24, May-24, and so on.
- **Labels.** `DateFormatter("%b-%y")` writes each date as a short month
  name and two-digit year, for example `Jan-24`, as in Excel's `mmm-yy`
  number format. `%b` is the month abbreviation and `%y` the year without
  century.
- **Vertical labels**, with tick marks pointing in.

### The y-axis

```python
ax.set_ylim(-10, 50)
ax.yaxis.set_major_locator(MultipleLocator(10))
ax.tick_params(axis="y", direction="in", length=2.8, pad=5)
```

From -10 to 50 with a tick every 10. The range is set wide enough for the
top of the band; growth of the total stays well within it.

The chart has no legend, because the subtitle and caption explain the single
line and the band.

## Changing the chart

- **Show all the data.** Move the left limit to
  `pd.Timestamp("2023-09-15")` and start the ticks in October 2023.
- **Label every month.** Use `freq="MS"`. With 30 months the labels will be
  crowded; every second or third month (`"3MS"`) is easier to read.
- **A different date format.** `"%m/%Y"` gives `01/2024`, `"%b %Y"` gives
  `Jan 2024`.

## The complete script

The full `python/fig-1-2-2.py`, as it runs:

```` {.python filename="python/fig-1-2-2.py"}
"""Figure 1.2.2: Remittances to CA4 Countries."""
import matplotlib.dates as mdates
import pandas as pd
from matplotlib.ticker import MultipleLocator

from chart_style import new_chart, read_chart_data, save_chart

STEM = "fig-1-2-2"

data = read_chart_data(STEM)
dates = pd.to_datetime(data["category"])

# In Excel the band is a stacked area: "Min" plus the "Min-Max Band" on top.
band_lower = data["Min"]
band_upper = data["Min"] + data["Min-Max Band"]

fig, ax = new_chart(
    title="Remittances to CA4 Countries",
    subtitle="(Year-over-year percent change)",
    caption=(
        "Sources: Haver Analytics; national authorities; and IMF staff calculations.\n"
        "Note: Nicaragua’s 2025–26H1 data are IMF staff estimates. CA4 =\n"
        "Central America 4 (El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua)."
    ),
    caption_size=7.8,
    left=0.4,
    right=0.2,
    bottom_gap=0.55,
)

ax.fill_between(dates, band_lower, band_upper, color="#FCE5D6", linewidth=0)
ax.axhline(0, color="#BFBFBF", linewidth=0.7)
ax.plot(dates, data["Total remittances"], color="#C55A11", linewidth=2.4,
        solid_capstyle="round", solid_joinstyle="round")

ax.set_xlim(pd.Timestamp("2023-12-15"), pd.Timestamp("2026-06-15"))
ax.set_xticks(pd.date_range("2024-01-01", "2026-05-01", freq="2MS"))
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%b-%y"))
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelrotation=90, direction="in", length=2.8, pad=5)

ax.set_ylim(-10, 50)
ax.yaxis.set_major_locator(MultipleLocator(10))
ax.tick_params(axis="y", direction="in", length=2.8, pad=5)

save_chart(fig, STEM)
````
